Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verses 1–3:

(p-147) Surat al-Hijr

It is Meccan by consensus, except for His saying: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] and the great Qur'an﴾, which is Medinan.

﴿Alif. Lam. Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ Regarding this there are two interpretations. The first: the Book is the Qur'an, and He combined for it the two names.

The second: the Book is the Torah and the Gospel, and then He linked them with "the clear Qur'an."

Regarding the meaning of "clear" (al-mubin) there are three aspects. The first: clear in its inimitability, so that it cannot be opposed.

The second: clear in distinguishing truth from falsehood, so that the two are not confused.

The third: clear in distinguishing the lawful from the unlawful, so that the two are not mixed up.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ Regarding the time of this wishing there are three opinions. The first: at the moment of witnessing in this world, when guidance becomes distinct to them from misguidance; this is what ad-Dahhak said.

(p-148) The second: on the Day of Resurrection, when they see the honour of the believers and the humiliation of the disbelievers.

The third: when the believer enters Paradise and the disbeliever enters the Fire.

Al-Hasan said: when the polytheists see the believers having entered Paradise while they themselves have gone to the Fire, they will wish that they had been Muslims.

"Perhaps" (rubba) is used in this place to mean "many," although it was originally laid down to mean "few," as the poet said:

Ah, perhaps the eye has sent you a glance, the most you get from it is that it does not benefit you.

Some scholars said that here too it is for "few" as well, because they said that this [wish] occurs in some situations and not in all of them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verse 4–5:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And We never destroyed a town but it had a known decree﴾. He means: never destroyed the people of a town.

﴿Except that it had a known decree﴾ may bear two meanings. One of them: a determined term (ajal).

The second: an inescapable obligation (fard mahtum).

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿No community can precede its term, nor can they delay﴾ may bear two meanings. One of them: their destruction does not come before its appointed term, nor does it come later than it.

The second: they do not die before the punishment so that they might find rest, nor is it delayed from them so that they might be safe.

And al-Hasan gave a third interpretation of it: no community precedes its messenger and its book, so that it is punished before them, and the messenger and the book do not come late to it.

(p-149) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We do not send down the angels except with truth﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions:

First: except with the Qur'an. This was said by al-Qasim.

Second: except with the message (al-risala). This was said by Mujahid.

Third: except with the decree of death for taking their souls. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Fourth: except with punishment if they do not believe. This was said by al-Hasan.

﴿And they would not have been given respite﴾, i.e., they would not have been delayed.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is We who sent down the Reminder﴾. Al-Hasan and al-Dahhak said: it means the Qur'an.

﴿And indeed, We are its guardian﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

First: "And indeed, We are guardians for Muhammad against whoever intends him harm among his enemies." This was related by Ibn Jarir.

Second: "And indeed, We are guardians of the Qur'an."

Regarding this guarding there are three opinions:

First: He preserved it until it is recompensed with it on the Day of Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan.

Second: He preserved it from Satan adding falsehood to it or removing any truth from it. This was said by Qatada.

Third: "Indeed, We are its guardians in the hearts of those for whom We desire good, and We remove it from the hearts of those for whom We desire evil."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verse 10–13:

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And We certainly sent (messengers) before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: al-shiya' (the sects) are the nations (al-umam). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second: al-shiya' is the plural of shi'ah, and the shi'ah is a group that is bound together and united in its word. So al-shiya' means factions (al-firaq). From this is His statement, exalted is He: ﴿or to confuse you into sects (shiya')﴾ [al-An'am: 65], meaning factions. Its root is derived from al-shiya', which is small firewood with which large logs are kindled, so it is the helper of the fire.

(p-150) The third: al-shiya' are the tribes. This was said by al-Kalbi.

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿Thus We cause it to enter into the hearts of the criminals.﴾ Regarding this there are four opinions. The first: thus We cause mockery to enter into the hearts of the criminals, even though they do not recognize it. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: thus We cause denial to enter into the hearts of the criminals. This was said by Ibn Juraij.

The third: thus We cause the Qur'an to enter into the hearts of the criminals, even though they do not believe. This was said by al-Hasan.

The fourth: thus, when the criminals deny it, We cause into their hearts that they do not believe in it.

His statement, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿They do not believe in it﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: they do not believe in the Qur'an that it is from Allah. The second: they do not believe in the punishment that will come upon them.

﴿And the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ Al-sunnah means the way or manner (al-tariqah). 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

"From the gazelles, his eyes and his manner, and his neck, the swift, proud one, when he neighed."

Regarding this there are two meanings. The first: the way of the former peoples has already passed, namely the punishment for those who persisted in denying the messengers.

The second: that they would not believe in their messengers when they were obstinate.

It may also carry a third meaning: that among them there were both believers and disbelievers.

It may also carry a fourth meaning: those who persisted in disbelief despite the miracles after the signs they had requested had come.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verse 14–15:

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿And if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they continued to ascend therein﴾. There are two interpretations of this:

(p-151) The first: "they" here refers to these polytheists, who continued to ascend through it. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: the angels continued to ascend through it while the polytheists were watching them. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.

His saying, Exalted and Majestic is He: ﴿they would surely say, "Our eyes have only been intoxicated (sukkirat)."﴾ Regarding ﴿sukkirat﴾ there are two readings: one with the consonant kaf doubled (shaddah), and the other without doubling it. Concerning the difference between them there are two views. The first: their meaning is one and the same. On this basis there are six interpretations:

The first: it means "were blocked up," related from al-Dahhak.

The second: "were blinded," related from al-Kalbi.

The third: "were seized," related from Qatadah.

The fourth: "were deceived," related from Juwaybir.

The fifth: "were covered and veiled," related from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla', and from it is the saying of the poet:

"And the sun rose over it, a helmet of light, and the eye of the heat-haze became intoxicated (tusakkaru)."

The sixth: its meaning is "were detained," related from Mujahid.

And from it is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

"They remained through a sleepless night, neither released nor intoxicated."

The second view: the meaning of sukkirat with doubling and without doubling differs. Concerning their difference there are two views. The first: without doubling it means "were bewitched," and with doubling it means "were seized."

The second: without doubling it is from the intoxication of drink (sukr al-sharab), and with doubling it is derived from "sakkartu al-ma'" (I dammed the water).

﴿Rather we are people bewitched (masḥūrūn)﴾. Regarding this there are three interpretations: The first: that is, "we have been bewitched, so we do not see."

The second: "misled (mudallalūn)," related by Thaʿlab.

(p-152) The third: "deluded (mufsidūn)."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verses 16–20:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We have placed in the sky great stars (burooj)﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions:

First: they are palaces in the sky in which there are guards. This was said by ʿAṭiyya.

Second: they are the stations (manazil) of the sun and the moon. This was said by ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā.

Third: they are the great stars, meaning the seven wandering planets (al-sayyara). This was said by Abū Ṣāliḥ.

Fourth: they are the stars. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatāda.

Fifth: they are the twelve constellations (al-burooj al-ithnā ʿashar).

The root of burooj is manifestation (al-ẓuhūr), and from it comes tabarrajat al-mar'a, meaning a woman displayed herself when she revealed herself.

﴿And We have adorned it for the observers﴾, that is, We made it beautiful.

﴿And We have guarded it from every accursed devil﴾, meaning the sky.

Regarding al-rajīm (the accursed) there are three aspects. First: it means the one cursed. This was said by Qatāda.

Second: the one stoned (al-marjūm) by a word or a deed, and from it is the saying of al-Aʿshā:

*yaẓallu rajīman li-rayb al-manūn wa-l-suqmu fī ahlihi wa-l-ḥazan*

The words of the Most High: ﴿And We created man from dry clay of black mud altered in form﴾. Here "man" (al-insan) refers to Adam, peace be upon him, according to the view of Abu Hurayrah and al-Dahhak.

As for al-salsal (dry clay), there are three opinions. The first is that it is dry clay that has not been touched by fire, so that when you strike it, it rings, and you hear a sound from it. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah, and from it comes the verse of the poet:

Many a barren plain where you see the clay within it, and beneath it the remnants of Bilal among the villages and the shoulders.

Al-salsalah is a loud sound heard from something other than a living creature, like the rattle of cloth.

The second is that it is clay mixed with sand. This is the view of Ikrimah.

The third is that it is foul-smelling clay. This is the view of Mujahid, derived from the saying "salla al-lahm wa asalla" (the meat became putrid and rotten) when it has rotted. The poet said:

That is a youth who gives of his worth, with whom meat does not spoil through the salul (decay).

Al-hama' is the plural of hamah, which is black, altered mud.

Regarding al-masnun (formed), there are seven opinions.

(p-158) The first is that al-masnun means foul-smelling and altered, from the saying "qad asinal-ma'u" (the water has become altered) when it changes. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, and from it comes the verse of Abu Qays ibn al-Aslat:

She gave my voice a drink of saliva, pure and unaltered, like musk mixed into the water of grape clusters.

The second is that al-masnun means set up and standing upright, from the saying "wajhun masnun" (a face that is shaped). This is the view of al-Akhfash.

The third is that al-masnun means poured out, from the saying "sanaytu al-ma'a ala al-wajh" (I poured the water over the face) when I poured it upon it. This is the view of Abu Amr ibn al-Ala'. From it is the narration reported from Umar that he used to pour water (yassunnu) over his face and not spill it (yashunnuhu). Ash-shunn is scattering water, and as-sunn is pouring it.

The fourth is that al-masnun is that which rubs against itself, from the saying "sananta al-hajar ala al-hajar" (I sharpened the stone against the stone) when I rubbed one against the other. From this the sharpening stone (al-misann) is named, because iron is sharpened on it. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The fifth is that al-masnun means fashioned.

The sixth is that it means moist. This is the view of Ibn Abi Talhah.

The seventh is that it means pure, from the saying "sinn sayfaka" (sharpen your sword), i.e., polish it.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verse 39–44:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿My Lord, because You have led me astray﴾, has three interpretations. The first: "because You have misguided me," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: "because You have deprived me of Your mercy."

The third: "because You have attributed to me the act of misguiding."

This statement of Iblis may carry two meanings. The first: that he says it in the form of an oath, its implied sense being: "By the truth of Your misguiding me."

The second: that he says it in the form of a conditional consequence, its implied sense being: "On account of Your misguiding me."

﴿I will surely make [evil] seem attractive to them on earth﴾ may carry two meanings. The first: I will surely make the committing of sins attractive to them.

The second: I will surely preoccupy them with the adornments of this world, distracting them from performing obedience.

(p-161) ﴿And I will surely mislead them all﴾, that is, I will surely lead them astray from guidance.

﴿Except for Your sincere servants among them﴾, and they are those who made their worship sincere, free from corruption or showing-off (riya'). Abu Thumama related that the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) asked 'Isa, peace be upon him, about the one sincere to God. He said: "The one who acts for God and does not like that people praise him."

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿He said, "This is a straight path to Me"﴾ has four interpretations. The first: its meaning is "This is a path that keeps its traveller straight until it brings him right to Paradise," said by 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: "This is a path leading to Me, straight," said by al-Hasan, so that ʿalayya (عَلَيَّ) carries the sense of ilayya (إلَيَّ, "to Me").

The third: that it is a warning and threat, its meaning being that its way is toward Me and its return is upon Me, like the saying of one who threatens and warns another: "Your way is upon me," said by Mujahid.

The fourth: its meaning is "This is a path whose straightness is upon Me through clear explanation and proof."

It was also said: through divine enabling (tawfiq) and guidance.

al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin read ﴿ʿalayya mustaqimun﴾ with the ya' raised and tanwin, and its meaning is "exalted and straight," i.e., exalted such that it cannot be attained, straight such that it cannot be made to incline.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verses 61–66:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿So set out with your family in a portion of the night﴾. In this there are three interpretations. The first: [it means] at the end of the night; this is what al-Kalbi said.

The second: [it means] at some part of the night; this is what Muqatil said.

The third: [it means] in the darkness of the night; this is what Qutrub said, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"And a wailing woman who laments in a portion of the night, over a man at the edge of the dust."

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And We decreed to him that matter﴾, meaning: We revealed to him that matter.

﴿That the last remnant of these people will be cut off by morning﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: their last [remnant]. The second: their root.

﴿Cut off by morning﴾, meaning: they will be uprooted by punishment at dawn.

(p-166) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿By your life, indeed they are wandering in their intoxication﴾. "By your life" (la'amruka) is an oath, and it has four interpretations:

First: its meaning is "by your life (wa-'aishika)." This is related from Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: its meaning is "by your deeds (wa-'amalika)." This was said by Qatadah.

Third: its meaning is "by your life (wa-hayatika)." This is also related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Allah Most High never swore by the life of anyone other than Him."

Fourth: "and by your right" (wa-haqqika), meaning the duty owed upon your community. The word 'amr here means "the truth," and from it comes their saying: la'amru Allah, meaning "and by the right of Allah."

As for ﴿in their intoxication﴾ (sakratihim), there are two interpretations:

First: "in their misguidance," said by Qatadah.

Second: "in their heedlessness," said by al-A'mash.

As for ﴿wandering﴾ (ya'mahun), there are four interpretations:

First: its meaning is "they waver" (yatarraddadun). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu Malik.

Second: "they dispute" (yatamarawn), said by al-Suddi.

Third: "they play" (yal'abun), said by al-A'mash.

Fourth: "they persist" (yumi'un), said by al-Kalbi.

(p-167) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed in that are signs for those who discern﴾. On this there are five interpretations. The first: "for those who perceive by insight (al-mutafarrisin)"; this is the view of Mujahid.

It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Beware of the insight (firasa) of the believer, for he sees by the light of God," and then he recited this verse. The second: "for those who take lessons (al-mu'tabirin)"; this is the view of Qatada.

The third: "for those who reflect (al-mutafakkirin)"; this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The fourth: "for those who look (al-nazirin)"; this is the view of al-Dahhak.

Zuhayr ibn Abi Sulma said:

"In them is a diversion for the friend, and a pleasing sight for the eye of the one who looks with discernment (al-mutawassim)."

The fifth: "for those who see (al-mubsirin)"; this is the view of Abu 'Ubayda.

al-Hasan said: "They are those who discern matters (yatawassamun al-umur)"

(p-168) so they know that the One who destroyed the people of Lot is able to destroy the disbelievers. From this is the saying of Abdullah ibn Rawaha to the Prophet ﷺ:

"I have discerned in you goodness, which I recognize, and God knows that my sight is sound."

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And indeed it is on a road that remains﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: "indeed it is a lasting destruction"; this is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The second: "indeed it is a well-marked road"; this is the view of Mujahid.

By His saying, He means: the cities of the people of Lot and the companions of the Thicket (al-Ayka), the people of Shu'ayb.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verse 78–79:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And indeed, the companions of the thicket were surely wrongdoers﴾. He means in their denial of the Messenger of God sent to them, who was Shu'ayb, for he was sent to two communities: the companions of the thicket (al-Aykah) and the people of Madyan.

The second is that it is intertwined trees, and most of their trees were al-dawm (the doum palm), which is al-maql. This is the view of Ibn Jarir, and from it is the saying of al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani:

Its two wings wipe off the cool dew from a dove of the thicket (ayka), its plumage stained with antimony (ithmid).

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿So We took vengeance upon them, and indeed, they both are on a clear highway﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: on a clear road, the saying of Qatadah.

It is said that the road is called "imam" because the traveler follows it (ya'tammu bihi) until he reaches his destination.

By His saying ﴿and indeed, they both﴾ he means the companions of the thicket and the people of Lot.

First: that it is turning away (al-i'rad) without impatience or distress.

Second: that it is forgiving them (safh) while still denouncing their disbelief and continuing to admonish them. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

Third: that it is pardoning them without rebuke or harshness.

Fourth: that it is contentment without reproach. This was said by Ali ibn Abi Talib.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And We have certainly given you seven of the oft-repeated [verses] (al-mathani) and the magnificent Qur'an﴾. On this there are five opinions.

First: the seven oft-repeated [verses] are the Opening chapter (al-Fatiha), so called because it is repeated each time the Qur'an is recited and prayed. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Abu al-'Aliya and al-Hasan.

It was also said: it is so called because the Most Merciful, the Compassionate (al-Rahman al-Rahim) is repeated in it. From this is the saying of the poet:

"I adjure you by the abode of the Qur'an, the Mother of the Book, the seven of the oft-repeated,
Repeated among the verses of the Qur'an, and the seven, the seven long ones that are wound around."

The second: they are the seven long [sūrahs]: al-Baqara, Al 'Imran, al-Nisa', al-Ma'ida, al-An'am, al-A'raf and Yunus. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: they were called al-mathani because stories, parables and lessons recur in them. It was also said: because they exceed the first hundred [verses] and reach into the second hundred.

Jarir said:

"May Allah reward al-Farazdaq when he wakes up neglecting al-Mufassal and al-Mathani."

The third: al-mathani refers to the entire Qur'an. This was said by al-Dahhak. From this is the saying of Safiyya bint 'Abd al-Muttalib lamenting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

"He was indeed a shining light by which one is guided,
Singled out with the revelation of the oft-repeated, the magnified."

The fourth: al-mathani are the seven meanings of the Qur'an: command, prohibition, glad tidings, warning, the coining of parables, the enumeration of blessings, and the reports of earlier generations. This was said by Ziyad ibn Abi Maryam.

The fifth: it is seven honours with which Allah honoured him: the first of them is guidance, then prophethood, then mercy, then compassion, then affection, then harmony, then tranquillity, and the magnificent Qur'an was added to them. This was said by Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with them both.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Do not strain your eyes toward what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them﴾. This means what We have given them of wealth.

Regarding His saying ﴿pairs of them﴾ there are three interpretations. First: they are the likes (al-ashbah). This was said by Mujahid.

Second: they are the kinds (al-asnaf). This was said by Abu Bakr ibn Ziyad.

Third: they are the wealthy (al-aghniya'). This was said by Ibn Abi Najih.

﴿And do not grieve over them﴾. On this there are two interpretations. One: do not grieve over them for the blessings I have bestowed upon them in their worldly life.

Two: do not grieve over what they will come to because of their disbelief.

﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾. On this there are two interpretations. One: be humble toward them. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Two: its meaning is to be gentle toward them. The poet said:

"And it suffices you that youths of a people's leader
Extend a wing over a brother in affliction."

The Lord's words: ﴿As We sent down upon the dividers﴾. Regarding them there are seven opinions:

First: They are the People of the Book, Jews and Christians, who divided the Qur'an and made it into parts (*a'da'*, meaning *ajza'*, portions). They believed in some of it and disbelieved in some of it. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: They are the People of the Book who divided the Qur'an in mockery of it. One of them said, "This surah is mine, and this surah is yours." Hence they were called "dividers" (*muqtasimin*). This is the view of 'Ikrimah.

Third: They are the People of the Book who divided their scriptures. Some of them believed in parts of them, while others believed in what the rest had disbelieved, and they disbelieved in what the others had believed. So God the Exalted named them "dividers." This is the view of Mujahid.

Fourth: They are the people of Salih who conspired together to kill him, and so they were called "dividers," as the Exalted said: ﴿They said, "Swear to one another by God that we will surely attack him and his family by night"﴾ [al-Naml: 49]. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: They are a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh who divided the roads of Makkah so that they could intercept those coming to it from the tribes, and turn them away from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by saying that he was a sorcerer, a poet, a soothsayer, or a madman, so that they would not believe in him. God the Exalted then sent a punishment upon them and destroyed them. This is the view of al-Farra'.

Sixth: They are a group of the disbelievers of Quraysh who divided the Book of God, making some of it poetry, some of it soothsaying, and some of it "the myths of the ancients." This is the view of Qatadah.

(p-173) Seventh: They are a people who swore oaths and bound themselves together by them. This is the view of al-Akhfash.

It is also said that they were al-'As ibn Wa'il, 'Utbah and Shaybah, the sons of Rabi'ah, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Umayyah ibn Khalaf, and Munabbih ibn al-Hajjaj.

The Lord's words: ﴿Who made the Qur'an into ʿiḍīn﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations:

First: It means "sects" or "groups." They made part of it poetry, part of it sorcery, part of it soothsaying, and part of it "the myths of the ancients." They thus made it into parts, as a slaughtered camel is cut into pieces (*yu'addā*). The word *ʿiḍīn* is the plural of *ʿuḍw* (a limb or part), derived from *'a·dai·tu al-shay'a ta'diyatan* (I divided the thing into parts) when I separated it. As Ru'bah ibn al-'Ajjaj said:

*Nor is the religion of God something divided into parts.*

meaning "something divided into pieces." This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak.

Second: The word *ʿiḍīn* is the plural of *ʿiḍah*, which is slander (*buhtān*). It derives from their saying *'a·ḍah·tu al-rajula a'ḍahuhu 'ḍhan* (I slandered the man) when I falsely accused him. They slandered the Book of God in what they accused it of. This is the view of Qatadah.

From this is the poet's line:

*Indeed, slander is not the deed of free men.*

Third: *ʿiḍīn* means mockers, because when the Qur'an mentioned the mosquito, the fly, the ant, and the spider, one of them said, "I am the owner of the mosquito," another said, "I am the owner of the fly," another said, "I am the owner of the ant," and another said, "I am the owner of the spider," mocking the Qur'an. This is the view of al-Sha'bi and al-Suddi.

Fourth: By *ʿiḍah* it is meant sorcery, because they made the Qur'an into sorcery. This is the view of Mujahid. The poet said:

*From their sorcery, you have a murmuring (zamzamah).*

meaning "from their sorcery."

'Ikrimah said: *ʿiḍah* is sorcery in the language of Quraysh, and they call a female sorceress *al-ʿāḍihah*. From this is what is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he cursed "the female sorceress (*al-ʿāḍihah*) and the woman who seeks to be made a sorceress (*al-mustaʿḍihah*)," meaning the female sorceress and the one who seeks sorcery.

(p-174) Regarding the derivation of *ʿiḍīn* there are two views. One is that it derives from *al-aʿḍā'* (the limbs or parts), which is the view of Ubaydah. The other is that it derives from *ʿiḍah*, which is sorcery, which is the view of al-Farra'.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 15, verse 94–99:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So proclaim openly what you are commanded﴾. Concerning it there are six interpretations:

First: "Proceed with what you are commanded," said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: its meaning is "make manifest what you are commanded," said by al-Kalbi.

A poet said:

"And who is one who openly speaks the truth after you, speaking with piety, and who, if injustice is spoken of, reproaches it?"

Third: it means "recite the Qur'an aloud in the prayer," said by Mujahid.

Fourth: it means "announce what is revealed to you until you convey it to them," said by Ibn Zayd.

Fifth: its meaning is "distinguish between truth and falsehood," said by Ibn 'Isa.

Sixth: its meaning is "divide the speech concerning them, whether they are gathered or alone," related by al-Naqqash.

Ru'bah said: "Nothing in the Qur'an is more grammatically eloquent (a'rab) than His saying ﴿So proclaim openly what you are commanded and turn away from the ignorant﴾." In it there are three aspects:

One: it is abrogated by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then kill the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: turn away from concern over their mockery.

Third: its meaning is with contempt for them, said by Ibn Bahr.

Then in it there are two aspects: one, "Make the truth manifest by what you are commanded regarding its proclamation."

Second: "Break falsehood by what you are commanded regarding its nullification."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾. They were five: al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, al-'As ibn Wa'il, Abu Zam'ah, al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, and al-Harith ibn al-Tulatilah.

As for al-Aswad ibn 'Abd Yaghuth, he came upon a branch of thorns which struck his eyes, so that his eyeballs ran down his face. He used to say: "Muhammad prayed against me and was answered, and I prayed against him and was answered: he prayed that I would be blinded, and I became blind; and I prayed that he would be an outcast in Yathrib, and so it was."

As for al-Harith ibn al-Tulatilah, he suffered from dropsy of the belly. "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had said to Jibril [when] he descended to him with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We have sufficed you against the mockers﴾: 'Leave my uncle to me'," meaning al-Aswad ibn al-Tulatilah.
